newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish parliament debates opening secret files.
newsitem.headline: Polish parliament debates opening secret files.

text.p: Polish legislators opened a heated debate on Thursday over whether to open up secret files to unveil former collaborators of the communist-era security police.

The bill on vetting public figures, proposed by a special parliamentary committee, divided the ruling leftist coalition of ex-communists and a peasant party and looked set to become a major topic in the run-up to parliamentary elections this year.
"The bill will reveal the past of politicians and public people, which should be transparent," deputy Bogdan Pek told parliament presenting the draft law.
"I hope the bill will become law before the elections...so that in the next parliament there will be no politicians whose past would not be known to the public," he added.
Poland, unlike some other former Soviet bloc countries such as the Czech Republic, has not revealed former agents of the communist security police since the old system collapsed seven years ago.

Many politicians, mostly from the right-wing opposition and the co-ruling Peasant Party (PSL), say this is a major set-back for nascent democracy because former collaborators of the ill-famed SB security service, who are vulnerable to blackmail, have taken important state jobs.

But others, notably members of the co-ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), argue it is too late for such an exercise and the Interior Ministry's archives are too unreliable to carry out a just vetting procedure.

"Is a fair vetting process possible in 1997? The answer must be negative...About 55 percent of the relevant files have been destroyed and we could point at agents with confidence only in 10 percent of cases," ex-communist deputy Jerzy Jaskiernia said during the parliamentary debate.

The bill, likely to go parliamentary committees for more scrutiny, would set up a special vetting court to probe whether candidates for state posts had been informers during the period of undemocratic rule between 1944 and 1990.

Candidates for top government, parliamentary, judicial and public media jobs would have to openly declare whether they had been informants of the now-disbanded SB, or the intelligence and counter-intelligence services, before taking a post.

They would face up to five years in prison, stiff fines and a ban from selected state jobs if the court found they had lied. But a declaration that they had collaborated would not in itself automatically block their way to such posts.

The bill is unlikely to be adopted in its current shape. Even if most Peasant deputies turn against their four-year-old coalition partners and help the opposition pass the bill, President Aleksander Kwasniewski is likely to veto it.

Kwasniewski, himself a former communist, and most cabinet ministers criticised the bill, saying it could harm security service operations because it permitted revealing intelligence and counter-intelligence agents.
Some opposition critics say the legislation does not go far enough because it would help unmask low-ranking agents while their masters from the communist party would remain unknown.
"The bill creates a net to catch minnows while it lets big fish free," said opposition deputy Piotr Marciniak.
